messages.subject: Re: Packrat and Source Control
messages.body_plain:
You'll also want to add .Rprofile, .Renviron, and the files under packrat.sources. Those are the files that redirect you to the private library (and support its population) when R starts up; without them, you won't use the private library by default when you pick up your project on another machine.

There's a little more detail in the Collaboration section of our walkthrough: http://rstudio.github.io/packrat/walkthrough.html

messages.subject: Re: Is this useful for deployments?
messages.body_plain:
I'll cautiously say yes--in fact the original motivation for Packrat was just such a scenario. However, the answer is somewhat dependent on your project and its dependencies.

If you're developing a proper R package which only depends on R packages on CRAN, it may be possible to do what you want without Packrat entirely, assuming the deployment environment has access to a CRAN mirror. If you declare your package's dependencies in its DESCRIPTION file, R's existing package installer (as well as extensions like devtools) can install those dependencies for you automatically when your package is installed.

Otherwise, yes, you can use Packrat to help you with deployment. Just copy your project directory to the target machine, start R in the target directory, and have it run initPackrat().

A couple caveats:
- Packrat can handle only R package dependencies--if your project has other kinds of dependencies, it won't be very helpful.
- Packrat installs only to a private library, not to the global directory -- so it's good for installing project dependencies, but if your goal is to deploy a *package* on which other code (outside the directory) depends, it's probably not the right tool.

We didn't cover it in the walkthrough, but there's a parameter called sourcePackagePaths that may be helpful in your case--you can use it to bundle a package you're currently working on as a dependency.

messages.subject: Re: Packrat and Source Control
messages.body_plain:
There is a workflow possible where you just checkin the lockfile, but it makes some presumptions.

In particular:

1. Every developer would have to install packrat manually before working with the project.

2. No packages could be used other than those currently available on CRAN and Github.

If you want to try it, you could checkin just the lockfile, and then when you pull the change on another machine you'd need to:

1. Install packrat

2. Run packrat::packify(dir) to add the .Renviron and .Rprofile files

3. Restart R in the directory

4. Run packrat::restore() to populate the library

Jonathan.

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm trying to use packrat with a collaborator — it seems like a really useful tool to avoid dependency hell! However, I'm having great difficulty setting it up. I've pulled his packrat.lock, packrat.sources/, .Rprofile and .Renviron files from Github, and attempted to set up the project to use packrat using initPackrat(), but this fails as follows:

> initPackrat()
Initializing packrat... OK
Installing abind (1.4-0) ... OK (downloaded binary)
Installing bitops (1.0-6) ... OK (downloaded binary)
Installing codetools (0.2-8) ... OK (downloaded binary)

Installing proto (0.3-10) ... OK (downloaded binary)
Installing RColorBrewer (1.0-5) ... OK (downloaded binary)
Installing RODBC (1.3-9) ... Error: Command failed (1)

This errors kills everything and stops the installation of packages that come alphabetically after RODBC and, if I understand it correctly, fails to initialise packrat at all. Is there a way to troubleshoot this error?

Also, packrat appears to duplicate the packages listed in the 'Packages' panel in RStudio, but doesn't actually load them. Would these duplications be cleared and packages loaded if packrat initialised correctly?

Many thanks for your help, and for this great tool!

Patrick.
